## 1. OPERATING STORY

### 1.1 The system in one narrative
**Plain-prose execution rule (D-028).** The VP triggers an objective by sending its objective record to the director. The director reads the objective, criteria, current ticket state, and applicable grants; it checks ownership and dependencies, writes the assignment and ticket transition through the controller, and sends the bounded work to the manager. The manager reads the assignment and ruleset, checks that its slice is authorized, writes the supervisor assignment, and receives a report. The supervisor reads the manager's conditions and evidence, checks the foreman's result against those conditions, and writes either a verified upward report or a blocked/waiting report. The foreman reads the work unit and criteria, checks its managed worker result, and writes the report and artifact references. A normal example is a release objective whose two evidence children finish before the director writes `accepted`. A failure example is a missing artifact: the supervisor writes `failed` or `blocked` with the missing reference, the director does not infer success, and an unknown remote run remains held for [reconcile](terminology.md#reconcile) rather than being replayed blindly.
The owner works through a **VP surface** — their own Hermes agent, or any surface speaking MCP/API/CLI to the director harness (RL-13, CT-10, DESIGN.md §11.1–11.2). The VP hands the director an **objective**: a requested outcome, not a task list. The director — a configured Hermes agent with its own skills, model, context window, and permission set (D-008) — owns the objective from that moment: it decomposes the objective, decides which managers owe which parts, and carries the VP's completion conditions downward.
Managers are configured agents too. Each manager takes the slice of the objective it owns, breaks it into **tasks**, and organizes supervisors in a task chat room. Supervisors execute **prescribed conditional rules** — they do not hold decision authority (D-003); they gather evidence, run bounded checks, and coordinate foremen. Foremen are the execution experts of the existing coding-hermes fleet: a foreman receives a task, describes and adjusts the work, manages and reallocates workers, and reports results (D-004). Workers execute single units of work.
Everything the hierarchy *says* lives in chat rooms backed by DuckBrain (RL-4/RL-5/RL-6): an objective **is** a room, a task **is** a room, every message is attributed and searchable, and every agent's wake ends in a report posted as a message (CT-05, §4.5 DESIGN.md). Everything the hierarchy *must remember to function* — rooms, messages, reports, session bonds, registry entries, limits, send manifests, **tickets and their transitions**, grants and session-policy snapshots — is CHD control state in the DuckBrain `chd` namespace (RL-15, CT-13). Work itself — code, worktrees, CI runs, worker sessions, local board files — lives where Hermes and the fleet already put it and is referenced by artifact refs in reports (§3.6; the F-002 boundary).
**Authoritative shared work state is in the control plane, not in a repository file** (D-021, R31-018). A ticket lives at `/chd/ticket/...`; agents read and update it through controller-routed tools. A local JSONL board may be exported or imported as a view, but it is never the authority and no agent commits/pulls it to synchronize with another agent. This replaces the rev-1.1 "two-touch-point" claim: the planes now touch at assignment in, result out, **and** ticket state read/write through the controller.
Native Hermes **session exports** are a third store (`chd-archive`), separate from control state and from room messages (D-017/D-018, R31-016). An export exists so a replacement agent can inspect what a lost session knew; it is not a live session and not a control record (the archive contract).
Admission has **two initiators** (D-022/D-029, R31-019). The scheduler remains the authority for timed work, and a supervisor may additionally (a) enqueue work for a later wake or (b) request immediate execution when the target gateway has capacity. Both paths use one durable reservation ledger; neither bypasses capacity, agent limits or permissions. The harness never spawns directly and never owns a clock (R-018, R-021): it registers ordinary scheduler triggers, answers their fire callbacks, accepts bounded run-now requests, and delivers every message to an agent as exactly one of the two Hermes delivery modes — NEW session or REUSE of the bonded session (CT-04, R-019). Session *provisioning* (fresh or fork) is a separate decision from delivery mode (VOL-B §7.5, VOL-C §4.1).
Every agent and every worker runs under its **own non-default Hermes profile** (D-023, R31-020). Profile identity is part of the agent's configuration (`hermesBinding.profile`), is bound to its gateway credentials, and is checked at session creation; a missing or shared profile fails closed. Profile isolation is not an OS sandbox — it separates session stores, memory and credentials, not privileges on the host.
Hermes owns the agent loop, persistent sessions, memory, learning, skill execution, model fallback, and profile behavior; CHD coordinates capable agents and never rebuilds those mechanisms (review Scope boundary; D-013 treats standing-rule integration as a Hermes dependency contract).
When work blocks, the blocker travels upward as evidence, not as a request to invent authority: a supervisor reports per its rules, a manager reports blocked, and the director — only if the VP authorized grant authority — may either reassign the blocked slice to a suitable manager or grant a permission from the VP-authorized pool (D-009). Ownership and evidence survive the move. When a manager reports completion, that is not acceptance: the director runs acceptance review against VP-supplied, director-derived, and standing-rule criteria, and only then does the objective move toward acceptance (D-010; detail of criteria/evidence contracts is VOL-D, F-013).

### 1.2 Federation operating story (R31-029, D-035)
**Plain-prose federation rule.** A director triggers federation by sending a scoped request through Crier. The receiving bridge reads the peer identity, local onboarding record, requested scope, and dedupe key; it checks local VP policy, writes the accept/deny/pending audit record, and forwards only an approved objective or report to the local director. Normal example: a correlated peer report updates the local ticket and returns the same peer request id. Failure example: a peer asks for an out-of-scope action; the bridge writes `403 peer_scope_denied` or `202 pending_local_approval`, produces no autonomous side effect, and preserves the request for review.
A deployment may include one owner coordinating several independent client directors, or two owners collaborating across their own director systems. These are examples of the federation contract, not a universal topology. Each owner retains a local VP, director, managers, supervisors, foremen, workers, control store and approval policy. A peer director is not a new internal hierarchy tier.
Crier is the transport between directors; it is not an authority bridge. The receiving director authenticates the configured `crier:<peer-id>` identity, looks up its operator-created onboarding record, and evaluates the requested objective/message/room/ticket scopes against local VP policy. The inbound request is mapped to a local peer actor with `origin=peer`, `peer_id`, and a stable `peer_request_id`; a remote `as: vp` claim is never accepted. Local VP precedence is absolute: the local VP is the only VP for local decisions, and a peer sender id cannot create or widen a grant. Delegated work uses the explicit GrantRecord and lineage rules in VOL-C §8.3; a peer trust record alone is not a VP grant.
The normal trace is: peer request → authenticated/scoped local actor → local approval or denial → local director ticket/objective → permitted downstream work → correlated report/reply. The correlation tuple carries `peer_request_id`, local `objective_id`/`ticket_id`, and `peer_report_id`. Retries reuse the peer request id and replay the mapping; duplicates do not make a second objective. Out-of-scope or untrusted work produces a durable denial (`403 peer_scope_denied`) or, when configured, `202 pending_local_approval` with no autonomous side effect. A bridge outage isolates federation traffic while local objectives continue. Internal reinvocation of the same local director is a separate local path, not autonomous peer federation.

### 1.3 What this volume specifies
- The six roles — VP, director, manager, supervisor, foreman, worker — with an explicit responsibility/authority matrix, delegated decision scopes, and the **four** independent authority classes (use / grant-use / meta-grant / subordinate-creation) (§2; F-003, R31-008, R31-026). - The per-agent non-default profile invariant and its consequences for identity, credentials and state (§1.1, §2.1; R31-020). - The hierarchy-to-foreman assignment/result contract and the four explicit boundaries — dual admission, managed worker dispatch, schedule control, durable storage with authoritative control-plane tickets (§3; F-002, R31-018/019/021). - The complete objective lifecycle: decomposition through acceptance, including dependencies, queue/blocked states, reassignment, cancellation, direction changes, cross-manager composition with separately delegated delivery, aggregation, and the wake-completion vs objective-completion distinction (§4; F-004, R31-009/010). - The master end-to-end flow and five role-pair contracts with inputs, triggers, actions, stores, calls, outputs, recipients and failure/rework paths (§5; R31-017). - A traced example skeleton that the acceptance demonstration must be able to instantiate end-to-end, naming the decision owner at every branch (§6).

### 1.4 Canonical terminology (defined once, linked everywhere)
These terms have exactly one meaning in the package; later volumes link here instead of redefining.
| Term | Meaning | |---|---| | `VP` | the owner's calling surface and the grant ceiling; not an org-chart tier | | director / manager / supervisor / foreman / worker | the six-role hierarchy of §2.1 | | `room` / `thread` | a DuckBrain key family and a `reply_to` tree inside it | | `task` | one bounded piece of work with one accountable owner | | `ticket` | the authoritative control-plane work item (VOL-E); a task's durable identity | | `workflow` | a registered, versioned state machine a ticket follows (VOL-E) | | `session` | a Hermes conversation (id minted by Hermes) | | `fork` | provisioning a new session from a parent session at a recorded point — **never a delivery mode** | | `bond` | CHD's durable join of (agent, room, subthread, work) to a Hermes session | | `attempt` | one dispatch episode of a send against one target session | | `run` | one worker execution record (`WorkerRun`, VOL-C §7.3) | | `gateway request` | exactly one HTTP POST to a Hermes gateway | | `send` | one logical owed piece of work, delivered by one or more attempts | | `report` | the exactly-one result message answering a send | | `dataset` | a schema-validated, queryable multirow report variant | | `grant` / `meta-grant` | a conferred right / the right to confer delegation rights | | `snapshot` | see [recovery terminology](terminology.md#snapshot); this volume uses the `SessionPolicySnapshot` record | | `archive` | a committed native session export in `chd-archive`; not a live session | | `checkpoint` | the coverage boundary (`checkpoint_seq`, `covered_through_ts`) of an archive | | `restore` | importing an archive into a new session; validated, never a blind DB copy | | `lease` | a capacity hold whose expiry is a **detection** deadline, not proof of stop | | `admission` | the durable capacity reservation that precedes dispatch | | `enqueue-only` / `run-now` | the two admission operations (§3.4, VOL-C §6.7) |
Two distinctions must survive into every later section:
- **send ≠ attempt ≠ gateway request.** A logical send may be attempted more than once, including against a fresh session; a gateway request is one POST. - **fork ≠ delivery mode.** Fork provisions a native session; delivery selects NEW or REUSE for a wake.

### 1.4 Master scenario and trace contract (R31-017, D-020)
This section is the readable master scenario. The normative handoff ledger in §5.1 is the machine-checkable companion: every row has all eight required fields, and the two traces below use the same ticket and event identities. The coding trace is `REL-412`; the non-coding trace is `BILL-77`. Neither scenario changes the generic ticket contract.

The ticket is the join key across both traces. A local worktree, spreadsheet, CI result, or other artifact is evidence linked from the ticket; it is never a replacement for the ticket state or transition event.

### Canonical review-log items consumed in this volume
- **Q-004 (answered).** When a manager cannot complete an assignment with its configured capabilities: report blocked upward; the director chooses an authorized permission change or reassignment; human escalation remains governed by configured approval and grant authority. Consumed as the normative shape of VOL-A-030/031/039 — the manager does not delegate to a peer on its own initiative. - **Q-006 (answered).** The director specifies the completion/approval condition **per assignment** and passes it down; continue-versus-wait follows existing human authorization, and an explicit stop-until-approval must hold. Consumed in VOL-A-015 (assignment contents), VOL-A-027 (criteria attach at decomposition) and VOL-A-037 (approval gates hold). - **Q-008 (answered).** Named role skill overrides are allowed when authorized by VP config or a valid on-demand director delegation; VP config prevails in conflict. Consumed in §2.1 (role composition) and VOL-A-010. - **Q-003 (partially answered).** Manager-creation and supervisor-creation are configurable permissions; **foreman/worker creation scope still requires contract clarification** — recorded as OW-1, reinforcing D-005's scope note. - **Q-007 (open integration clarification; do not block).** The NEW/REUSE event mapping is an open integration item owned by VOL-B (F-010); this volume references the two delivery modes only as Hermes-backed facts and does not block on the mapping (OW-7). - **Hermes gateway facts (review-log `hermes_gateway_check`, official docs).** Hermes provides REST session creation, continuation, metadata/history and forks; continued sessions retain memory-provider recall between turns; named profile routing binds authentication to the routed profile. These are the platform contracts NEW/REUSE maps onto (CT-04, F-010 → VOL-B) — CHD does not rebuild them. Caveat consumed in VOL-A-036: Hermes documents **session-start frozen memory snapshots**, so immediate propagation of newly learned standing rules to in-flight sessions is not guaranteed — acceptance requires effective-rule evidence, not assumed propagation (D-013). - **DuckBrain dependency corrections (review-log `correct_duckbrain`, wojons/ duckbrain rev 972aeb0).** Memory keys **must start with `/`** — key examples in this volume are normalized to `/chd/...` (older shapes in DESIGN.md and the contracts, written without the leading slash, need the same normalization at the VOL-B record contracts, F-019). Same-key writes create **independent versions** and the buffered default durability has **no power-loss barrier** — key-version selection and the durability/ack contract are record-layer matters pinned in VOL-B (F-007/F-019); this volume's control-state requirements (VOL-A-023/ 024/025) require that VOL-B contract to exist, and no key in this volume relies on default timestamp ordering.

## 2. ROLE AUTHORITY MODEL (F-003)

### 2.1 The six roles
CHD defines exactly six roles. The first three are hierarchy roles inside the director harness's own configuration (DESIGN §3.2, DATA-MODEL §1.1); the foreman and worker are the fleet's existing execution tier reached *through* the hierarchy; the VP is a caller role outside the org chart (RL-13).
1. **VP** — the owner's calling surface (owner's Hermes agent via its director-calling tool, Claude Code, MCP/API/CLI/webhook callers, the scheduler acting as VP, the UI chat send box) (RL-13, CT-10, CT-14, §11.2 DESIGN.md). Gives direction to the director; holds the grant ceiling. 2. **Director** — the single hierarchy decision owner (D-003). Organizes managers, owns final decisions, delegates decision scope to managers, runs acceptance review, and escalates to the VP when ambiguity or authority limits are reached. 3. **Manager** — organizes supervisors for a slice of an objective (D-001). Makes decisions **within the delegated decision scope the director granted it** (D-003); escalates ambiguity upward rather than expanding its own authority. Some managers may create supervisors per configuration (D-009). 4. **Supervisor** — executes **prescribed conditional rules** for bounded work and coordinates foremen (D-001, D-003). A supervisor's rules can send it to check, gather, verify, compare, and report — they cannot silently acquire manager authority (F-003 completion evidence). 5. **Foreman** — execution expert for a work area (D-004). Receives a task, describes and adjusts the work, manages and reallocates workers, verifies their output, and reports upward. The foreman's operating loop is the existing coding-hermes-foreman skill machinery (board reads, worktrees, worker dispatch, gates) — CHD does not redesign it (§3 of this volume). 6. **Worker** — executes a single assigned unit of work and reports to its foreman. Workers hold no hierarchy authority and no hierarchy messaging duties: they reach the hierarchy only through their foreman.
**Apparent sub-directors are not a seventh tier.** What looks like a sub-director is an invocation of the same director under a different room or cycle (D-015); no additional hierarchy tier exists between director and managers.
**Roles are configurations, not ranks.** Each director, manager, supervisor, foreman and worker is a configured AI agent with its own toolset, permission list, workspace, approval policy, provider/model, context settings and **its own non-default Hermes profile** (D-008, D-015, D-023). Two agents sharing a profile is a validation error (`profile_shared`), and any agent running in `default` is a conformance failure: sessions, memory and credentials must be attributable per agent (R31-020; contract VOL-D §1.6/§2). Role composition (project instructions + base role template + named specialization, with authorized specialization overriding base behavior) is a configuration-contract matter (VOL-D Pt I); this volume pins only the authority consequences: a named specialization may override base role behavior/permissions **when authorized** (D-016; Q-008: overrides allowed when authorized by VP config or valid on-demand director delegation), and precedence is VP-configuration > director delegation (D-016, Q-008).

**Allowed-request set (R31-008):** a supervisor may request only `chd_assign` for a foreman already assigned in its task room, with `admission=enqueue_only|run_now`, `ticket_id`, `assignment_id`, `room`, `thread_root`, instruction/criteria refs, and its own authorization proof. The controller checks the assignment edge, current profile readiness, gateway/agent capacity, and the shared reservation atomically. A supervisor cannot create agents, dispatch workers, mutate lanes, change permissions, or target another supervisor's room. This list is identical to VOL-C §8.2 and ENDPOINTS §4.11.
**VOL-A-041 (matrix completeness, R31-008).** The matrix SHALL distinguish four different acts that rev 1.1 conflated: **control-plane agent creation**, **work-plane worker launch**, **request-wake** (enqueue for a later wake) and **direct scheduling** (mutating lanes). The foreman SHALL appear as a principal with the permissions it needs to report and to dispatch its own workers; a supervisor SHALL be able to perform exactly the requests its written workflow names (assign/enqueue/run-now/wake) without hitting an "enforced deny". The enforced implementation matrix is VOL-C §8.2; the two tables agree row for row.
**VOL-A-001** (F-003, D-001, D-003, D-004): CHD SHALL define exactly the six roles above; every hierarchy message, decision, and report SHALL name an agent whose role is one of the six, and apparent sub-director activity SHALL be attributed to the single director agent (D-015). *Evidence obligation: a traced task names the decision owner at every branch.*
**VOL-A-002** (F-003, D-003): Decision authority SHALL follow the matrix: the director owns all final decisions except the decision scope it explicitly delegated to a named manager; a supervisor's execution SHALL be limited to its prescribed conditional rules; a supervisor action SHALL never widen a manager's delegated scope. Ambiguity beyond written scope SHALL escalate upward (D-003), never be resolved sideways.
**VOL-A-003** (F-003, D-004): The foreman's execution expertise SHALL be preserved as an authority in its own right: given a task, the foreman decides how the work is described, adjusted, split across workers, reallocated mid-flight, and verified — CHD coordinates the foreman through assignment and result contracts (§3) and SHALL NOT prescribe the foreman's internal work-management steps.

### 2.3 Delegated decision scope
**VOL-A-004** (F-003, D-003, D-008): Each manager's delegated decision scope SHALL be explicit configuration data (part of the agent config the VP/operator owns; D-008), naming the decision classes the manager may commit (e.g. task ordering, worker-wave sizing, board-row selection within its responsibility domain) and the classes it may not (e.g. changing completion conditions, granting permissions, cross-domain reassignment). The default where config is silent SHALL be **no delegated decision scope** (deny-by-default, matching DESIGN §6.1's grant posture).
**VOL-A-005** (F-003, D-003): A manager operating beyond its delegated scope — including a decision that produces a report claiming an outcome its scope cannot authorize — SHALL produce an incident path: the harness/verify loop treats the out-of-scope commitment as `bad_report` material per CT-06/§5.1 mechanics (owned in detail by VOL-D), and the decision itself is void pending director or VP action.

### 2.4 Supervisor conditional actions — rules, not authority
**VOL-A-006** (F-003, D-003): A supervisor's behavior SHALL be expressed as prescribed conditional rules of the form *condition → bounded action → report*. Bounded actions are: read/check a named artifact, run a bounded verification probe, gather evidence, compare against a rule threshold, post a message, wake the manager, coordinate a foreman per the task room's assignment. A supervisor SHALL NOT: open rooms, create agents, grant permissions, reassign tasks to other managers, alter completion conditions, or commit any decision class named in a manager's delegated scope (VOL-A-004).
**VOL-A-007** (F-003): A supervisor rule whose condition cannot be resolved by the written rules (ambiguous evidence, contradictory conditions, threshold unknown) SHALL produce an escalation message to its manager with the evidence attached — never a improvised decision. This is the mechanical meaning of "supervisors execute prescribed conditional rules rather than receiving decision authority" (D-003).

### 2.5 The four distinct permission classes
The review requires that use, grant, meta-grant and subordinate-creation permissions are never inferred from one another (D-009, D-032). This volume pins the semantics and the pools; enforcement contracts (service-boundary checks, audit, revocation readback) are VOL-C §8 (F-012, R31-026).
**VOL-A-008** (D-009, D-032, F-003, F-012): CHD SHALL model four independent permission classes per agent: - **use** — the agent may exercise the capability itself; - **grant-use** — the agent may confer a capability from a named allowed pool onto a named subordinate; - **meta-grant** — the agent may confer the right to delegate further (make another grantor), bounded by recipient scope and downstream rights; - **subordinate-creation** — the agent may create instances of a named tier.
Possession of any one class SHALL NOT imply another. An agent MAY hold grant authority for a capability it cannot itself use (D-009: "an agent may have authority to grant a capability from an allowed pool without having permission to exercise that capability itself"); this MUST be validated in the acceptance demonstration (handoff: "a grantor authorized to grant a tool it cannot use").
**VOL-A-042 (meta-grant semantics, R31-026).** A meta-grant SHALL name the capability, resource scope, permitted recipients and allowed downstream rights. A grantor SHALL NOT confer a meta-grant broader than its own, SHALL NOT issue one without citing the authority that permits it, and SHALL NOT create a cycle. The grant lineage (VP root → … → issued grant) SHALL be durable and readable at both ends. A director may not use a meta-grant to escape a VP denial: VP configuration remains the root (VOL-A-010). Enforcement, rejection codes and readback are VOL-C §8.3 (VOLC-068).
**VOL-A-009** (D-009, F-003, F-012): Each grant-class grant SHALL name its **allowed pool** explicitly: the set of capabilities grantable, the tiers of grantee permitted, and any scope limits (rooms, workdirs, duration). Empty pool = no grant authority. The pool's ceiling is set by VP configuration; a director may sub-delegate only inside it (D-016: VP configuration wins conflicts with director delegation).
**VOL-A-010** (D-016, F-003): Permissions configured by the VP in agent config SHALL require no director grant — they are already VP grants (D-016). Director on-demand grants apply only to changes within its delegatable authority, SHALL carry provenance (`origin: vp-config | director-grant:<send/id>`), and SHALL lose to VP configuration on any conflict (D-016). Skill wording alone SHALL NOT be read as an effective permission grant (F-012 boundary; enforcement VOL-C).
**VOL-A-011** (D-005, D-009, F-003): Subordinate-creation SHALL be governed by explicit settings: `director.created-managers = on/off` (D-005: managers are typically predefined; a setting can permit the director to create managers; **default is OPEN DESIGN WORK** — §8, OW-2) and per-manager `created-supervisors = on/off` (D-009: "some managers may create supervisors according to configuration"). Foremen and workers below the supervisor tier SHALL NOT be created by any hierarchy agent in this revision; lower-tier creation policy is **OPEN DESIGN WORK** (D-005 scope note; §8, OW-1).

### 2.6 Escalation paths
**VOL-A-012** (F-003, D-003, D-009): Every escalation SHALL be a durable incident record in the parent room (R-017: an escalation that leaves no record is a defect). The canonical ladder is DESIGN §7.3: agent blocked/failed → parent agent room (incident message) → director (aggregates; may re-send or defer subtree) → owner page at the DESIGN.md §7.3 triggers. Role-specific escalation reasons in this volume's lifecycle: ambiguity beyond decision scope (VOL-A-002, VOL-A-007), blocked work (D-009), waiting-for-human (D-012), authority limits on grants (VOL-A-009: a needed grant outside the allowed pool escalates to the holder of the larger pool, ultimately the VP).

### 2.7 Revocation paths
**VOL-A-013** (F-003, F-012 boundary; **superseded in part by VOL-A-043**). Revocation SHALL mirror grant origin: the VP (via config change, taking effect per config-activation rules — VOL-D §1.1) revokes VP-configured permissions; a director-granted permission is revoked by the granting agent or by VP override (VP configuration wins conflicts, D-016). Revocation SHALL be recorded with provenance so effective-policy readback shows the current state. A director SHALL NOT revoke a VP-configured permission by issuing a conflicting delegation. The rev-1.1 rule that scheduled permission revocation for the session's following turn is **superseded** (RETIRED, not quoted here — retired wording preserved in the retained review evidence under `evidence/r32-review/inputs/` so the package contains no live occurrence of the retired wording) by VOL-A-043 for session-scoped rights.
**VOL-A-043 (session-lifetime revocation, R31-027, D-033, D-038).** Revocation SHALL operate at the **session boundary**, not the request boundary:
1. Every session holds a `SessionPolicySnapshot` (VOL-B §3.11) captured at creation and at every fork; effective enforcement for that session reads the snapshot. 2. An **existing** session retains the permissions that were effective for it when it started. A revoked ancestor grant does not reach into it. 3. A **future** session (new session, new fork, replacement, restore without a snapshot) resolves current valid grants: rights derived from revoked authority are absent; independent VP grants keep their own origin and remain. 4. A fork follows the configured `sessions.fork_policy`: `preserve_parent_snapshot` (default) copies the parent snapshot verbatim, `current_policy` resolves at fork time. 5. An explicit, authorized **policy resync** is the only way an existing session's effective set changes; it is never automatic, never triggered by a tool call. 6. "Existing vs future" is defined exactly as above across fork, restart, replacement and restore; a restore that cannot find the archived snapshot fails closed to `current_policy` and records `snapshot_missing`. 7. A revoked grantor MAY still hold `use` in its existing session, but SHALL NOT be able to issue new downstream grants: issuance is evaluated against current authority, not the snapshot. This edge is explicit, not inferred.
The operations, errors and readback are VOL-C §8.9; the acceptance variants are WF-08 plus the D-038 session-policy tests in `acceptance/`.

## 3. HIERARCHY-TO-FOREMAN INTEGRATION BOUNDARIES (F-002)

### 3.1 The reconciliation problem, stated
Three rules collide at the foreman tier:
1. The review requires foremen/workers **beneath the supervisor tier** (F-002, D-001). 2. The **foreman skill** (coding-hermes-foreman, read 2026-11-08) runs a delivery loop that: reads JSONL boards with `boardctl`, dispatches workers by launching CLI sessions (`hermes chat -q …` from inside the foreman's own session — the pattern recorded as FACT-23 in DESIGN.md), creates git worktrees, runs GitReins judges, and performs **self-pause** and schedule- adjacent actions in its own tick loop. 3. CHD norms say: agents never self-schedule (R-021), nothing reaches a gateway except through the harness (R-023 two-hop rule), and DuckBrain is the only durable store **for CHD control state** (RL-15 as scoped by the review: "DuckBrain-only persistence means CHD control state only").
The resolution is a **two-plane model**: the foreman simultaneously lives in CHD's *control plane* (as an addressable agent that receives assignments and owes reports through rooms) and in the fleet's *work plane* (its existing tick loop, board, worktrees, workers). The planes touch at exactly two points — assignment in, result out — and the boundaries below name what each plane owns.
**VOL-A-014** (F-002): CHD SHALL treat a foreman as a two-plane agent: in the control plane it is a room-member agent that receives task assignments and posts reports (CT-05 semantics); in the work plane it is the existing foreman skill loop whose internals (board reads, worktree creation, worker dispatch, judges, gates) are outside CHD's contracts. CHD SHALL NOT re-specify, wrap, or replace the foreman skill's internal loop.

### 3.2 Assignment contract (control plane → foreman)
**VOL-A-015** (F-002, D-001, D-004): A foreman assignment SHALL be a task-room message (kind `task`, per DATA-MODEL §1.4) posted by the coordinating supervisor's side of the task room — concretely: the supervisor coordinates foremen per D-001, and the assignment message carries: the objective id and task room, the bounded work description, the completion conditions passed down **unchanged** from the director's assignment unless an authorized change is recorded (D-012; criteria-provenance detail VOL-D F-013), the artifact expectations, and the completion/approval condition the director specified for this assignment, passed down unchanged (Q-006, D-012; criteria-provenance detail VOL-D F-013), and the report deadline implied by `verify.deadline_s` (DESIGN §5.1). Assignment delivery to the foreman's session uses the same two-mode NEW/REUSE path as every other agent (CT-04) — the foreman's gateway/session plumbing is unchanged fleet plumbing (FACT-11).
**VOL-A-016** (F-002, D-004): Within one assignment, the foreman MAY issue multiple progress messages and SHALL post exactly one final report per owed send (CT-05: zero or more chat messages, exactly one report message per wake). The foreman's report follows the DATA-MODEL §1.5 report shape (`status: done|deferred|blocked|failed`, artifacts required for `done`, freshness rule RL-20).

### 3.3 Result contract (foreman → control plane)
**VOL-A-017** (F-002): A foreman result SHALL reach the hierarchy only as a report/progress message in its task room (CT-05), authenticated with its role token (FACT-19/FACT-20); the verify loop (CT-06) and the missing-reply ladder (CT-11, RL-11) apply to foreman sends exactly as to supervisor sends. Artifact references in the report (board row ids, commit shas, CI run ids) point INTO the work plane; the harness samples artifact existence per DESIGN §4.5/M5.

### 3.4 Boundary 1 — Admission (two initiators, one ledger)
**VOL-A-018** *(superseded by VOL-A-044 — kept for lineage; the scheduler-only reading must not survive anywhere.)*
**VOL-A-044 (dual admission, R31-019, D-022/D-029).** A foreman wake SHALL be admitted through exactly one of two initiators:
1. **Timed** — the harness's registered trigger lane fires, the harness composes the send, and admission follows the configured path (scheduler bump or controller-local reservation; VOL-C §6.7 records which). 2. **Requested** — a supervisor (or a director on a delegated path) calls `chd_assign` with `admission: enqueue_only | run_now`. `enqueue_only` places the work for a later wake; `run_now` attempts immediate execution.
Both initiators share one durable capacity ledger derived from send manifests (no second counter), one dedupe identity per request, and one atomic reservation primitive; concurrent requests for the same assignment resolve to one dispatch and the loser receives the winner's ids (VOL-C §6.7). Neither path may exceed per-gateway `max_inflight`, per-agent `max_sessions`, or permissions. No hierarchy agent may mutate scheduler lanes (VOL-A-022).

### 3.5 Boundary 2 — Worker launching
Rev 1.1 said the foreman launches workers by CLI from inside its own session (FACT-23). That prescription is **superseded** (D-024, R31-021): CLI-launched Hermes inherits the foreman's environment, profile and provider, which contradicts the per-agent profile invariant (§2.1). Workers are launched through a managed, structured dispatch.
**VOL-A-019** *(superseded by VOL-A-045 — kept for lineage; no CLI worker launch is conforming.)* **The managed dispatch contract is the only live rule.**
**VOL-A-045 (managed worker dispatch, R31-021, D-024).** A foreman SHALL dispatch workers only through `chd_worker_dispatch` (controller endpoint `POST /v1/workers/dispatch`, VOL-C §7). The request names the worker and its non-default profile, the work records (ticket/assignment/room/thread/send), the instruction reference, the workspace, and optionally the runtime settings. The controller validates authority, profile distinctness, workspace scope and capacity, creates a durable `WorkerRun`, and executes the gateway POST. The foreman receives a `run_id`, observes progress and result asynchronously, and verifies the result itself (D-004). A worker run is **not** a hierarchy send: it is a work-plane execution whose result reaches the hierarchy only as the foreman's report (VOL-A-017).
**VOL-A-020** (F-002, R-021): Hierarchy agents SHALL NOT acquire schedule control through worker launching. The foreman's own tick cadence and self- pause behaviors, as implemented by the existing skill and governed today by the scheduler's admission/cooldown machinery (FACT-01/FACT-05/FACT-06), remain exactly as they are; CHD neither grants nor audits them as hierarchy actions. A foreman's *self-pause of its fleet lane* is a work-plane event: if it bears on a CHD assignment, it surfaces as a `deferred`/`blocked` report reason, not as a CHD schedule mutation.
**VOL-A-021** (F-002 — OPEN DESIGN WORK, narrower in rev 2.0): the dispatch contract now states the fields a foreman reports (run ids, progress, result, artifacts), because the run record makes them observable. Still OPEN: whether worker-run counts feed typed caps (`max_parallel` per role) or remain advisory, and whether a foreman may hold `create_worker` to provision a new worker profile without an operator. Until decided, the foreman may dispatch **existing** workers only; worker profile creation stays operator-owned (§8, OW-3).

### 3.6 Boundary 3 — Schedule control
**VOL-A-022** (F-002, R-021, CT-08): No hierarchy role — including foremen — may create, alter, or delete scheduler lanes as a hierarchy action. An agent that wants a future wake asks the harness (CT-08). Foreman skill behavior that touches schedule-adjacent state (self-pause, lane prompts) is work-plane behavior owned by the existing scheduler/config machinery, unchanged by CHD.
**Capacity and lease rule (R31-006).** Schedule admission and caps are governed by VOL-B §6.4/§6.7's manifest-derived ledger. A lease expiry is only a bounded reconciliation trigger: it is never proof that a remote run stopped and never by itself releases a gateway or agent slot. The run-status owner must obtain a terminal run result or correlated terminal report before release; `running`, `unknown`, and `unreachable` retain the slot. In a partition where the old harness may still execute, a second harness is refused by the writer-lease startup gate (VOL-B §4.4), so availability is sacrificed before exceeding the configured cap.
Schedule ownership restatement: no hierarchy role — including foremen — may create, alter, or delete scheduler lanes as a hierarchy action. An agent that wants a future wake asks the harness (CT-08). Foreman skill behavior that touches schedule-adjacent state (self-pause, lane prompts) is work-plane behavior owned by the existing scheduler/config machinery (FACT-07/FACT-15), unchanged by CHD. The hierarchy's only schedule instrument is trigger registration and wake requests by the harness itself (CT-02, CT-08).

### 3.7 Boundary 4 — Durable storage: control state vs work artifacts
**VOL-A-023** (F-002, RL-15 scoped, revised for D-021): The DuckBrain-only invariant SHALL apply to **CHD control state**: room/message/report keys, registry mirrors, session bonds, limits, send manifests, **tickets and ticket events, grants and policy snapshots** (DATA-MODEL §2 / VOL-B §2 key families). The following SHALL be explicitly OUTSIDE the invariant and stay where the existing machinery puts them: - **local** board files and GitReins task records used as working views (they are exports/imports of ticket state, never the authority — VOL-A-046); - git worktrees, commits, CI runs and their evidence; - worker sessions and their Hermes session storage (Hermes-owned); - agent memory, skill files, and learned context (Hermes-owned — review Scope boundary: "distinguish native Hermes memory/session/skill storage and work artifacts"). Control-plane references to work-plane state are artifact *refs* in reports (DATA-MODEL §1.5 `artifacts`), never copies.
**VOL-A-046 (authoritative shared tickets, R31-018, D-021).** Shared work state SHALL live in the control plane and be accessed through controller-routed tools (VOL-E). A local board file SHALL be treated as a mirror/import view: it may be regenerated from the ticket store, may not be edited as authority, and is never synchronized between agents by commit/pull. Two agents reading/updating one ticket do so through the controller; transitions are authorized and revision-checked (`expected_revision`, VOLE-009); a restart preserves committed state because the store, not the working copy, holds it. This replaces the rev-1.1 claim that the planes touch at exactly two points: ticket reads and updates are additional control-plane interactions, and they are enumerated in VOL-E §3.
**VOL-A-024** (F-002): A CHD component that requires durable hierarchy authority data (assignment ownership, delegated scopes, grant provenance, objective state) SHALL store it as CHD control state under the VOL-B record contracts (F-006) — never in work-plane files (boards, repos) and never in Hermes memory. Conversely, work products SHALL NOT be duplicated into DuckBrain "just in case"; the room log carries the reference and the accountable summary (RL-6: the report arrives as a message).

### 3.8 The full assignment/result loop, drawn
**Plain-prose loop explanation.** The manager triggers an assignment by writing a task-room message. The router reads membership and wake targets; the harness checks admission and profile authority, writes the send manifest, and dispatches through the gateway. The foreman reads the work unit and criteria, manages the worker, checks returned artifacts, and writes one final report to the room. A normal example is a worker commit linked to a verified report that closes the send. A failure example is a report with the wrong ticket or missing artifact: the harness writes `bad_report` or `blocked`, keeps the ticket open, and reports the exact evidence instead of re-deriving success from a wake. The arrow `router → wake target` is routing only; DuckBrain never wakes the gateway.

### 4.2 Decomposition and assignment ownership
**VOL-A-026** (F-004, D-001, D-003): The director decomposes each objective into manager assignments; each assignment names exactly one **accountable owner** manager (one owner per deliverable — F-009's rule, restated as a lifecycle invariant), the completion conditions carried down (D-012), and any dependencies on sibling assignments. Decomposition is a director decision class (VOL-A-002); a manager may further decompose its slice into tasks for supervisors, but ownership of the manager-level deliverable does not transfer without director action (reassignment, §4.6).
**VOL-A-027** (F-004, D-010, Q-006): The director SHALL define acceptance criteria when the VP supplied none, and may extend supplied criteria to cover additional requirements (D-010). Criteria provenance (`vp-supplied`, `director-derived`, `standing-rule`) and versioning are VOL-D (F-013); lifecycle-wise, criteria attach to the objective at `decomposing` and every downstream assignment carries the director-specified conditions unchanged unless an authorized change is recorded (D-012, F-013).

### 4.3 Dependencies
**VOL-A-028** (F-004): Assignments MAY declare dependencies on sibling assignments (`depends_on`, mirroring the fleet board concept at K2). A dependent assignment SHALL NOT be dispatched to its manager while any dependency is unsatisfied (definition in VOL-A-049); dependency readiness is checked at send composition (harness mechanics, CT-13/§3.4 DESIGN.md) and reflected in the objective state (`queued` when cap-waiting, `blocked` when a dependency is unsatisfied and will not resolve without action).
**VOL-A-049 (dependency satisfaction ≠ terminality, R31-009).** Terminality is not success. A dependency is **satisfied** only when its producing assignment ends in `accepted` (or `reported` + verified) **and** supplies the artifact the dependent work needs. Outcomes are classified:
| Dependency outcome | Releases dependent work? | What happens | |---|---|---| | `accepted` with required artifact(s) | yes | normal dispatch | | `accepted` without a required artifact | no | dependent reports `blocked{reason: missing_prerequisite_artifact}` | | `cancelled` | **no** | dependent does **not** silently proceed; it becomes `blocked{reason: prerequisite_cancelled}` and the director decides | | `failed` | no | dependent blocks; ladder/escalation applies | | `expired` (producing send closed `closed{expired}`, or its wait lapsed) | **no** | dependent holds; the director re-dispatches the expired producer or cancels the dependent | | replaced by a documented replacement assignment | yes, when the replacement is `accepted` and supplies the artifact | the dependency edge is re-pointed to the replacement (`replaces` field), recorded with the director's authority |

**VOL-A-050 (cancellation propagation).** Cancelling an assignment SHALL mark every direct dependent `blocked` with `prerequisite_cancelled`, notify the owning manager, and leave the objective aggregate `blocked` until the director either (a) records a replacement assignment, (b) re-scopes the dependent, or (c) cancels the dependent. A cancelled prerequisite never "releases" dependent artifact work merely by being terminal, and a dependent never invents a substitute artifact.
This is a coordination contract, not agent reasoning: the harness computes satisfaction from records; an agent may not declare a dependency satisfied.

### 4.4 Queue and blocked states
**VOL-A-029** (F-004, RL-15): `queued` is a normal, counted state: scheduling is always allowed; a cap-full gateway queues the send (`429 at_capacity`, message persisted, wake queued — ENDPOINTS §4.2/§5). Queue aging and the `deferred{reason: backpressure}` close are DESIGN §3.4. Queueing is never a failure of the objective and SHALL NOT trigger the failure ladder by itself.
**VOL-A-030** (F-004, D-009, D-012, Q-004): `blocked` SHALL always carry structured evidence: what blocks, who owns the unblock, and what authority would be required (reassignment? a grant? human input?). The reporting agent keeps ownership of the blocked work until the director acts — a blocked report does not silently transfer or drop the assignment. A manager blocked on capability reports upward; it does not delegate to a peer on its own initiative (Q-004).

### 4.5 Reassignment, cancellation, changed VP direction
**VOL-A-031** (F-004, D-009, Q-004): On a blocked escalation, the director may (1) reassign the blocked slice to a suitable manager/team, or (2) grant a permission — only if the VP authorized that grant authority and the capability is in the allowed pool (D-009, VOL-A-009; the director's grant-or-reassign choice is the Q-004 ruling). Reassignment transfers the assignment record with its full evidence trail to the new owner; the prior owner's reports and artifacts remain in the room log and remain referenced by the objective record. Ownership and evidence are preserved across the move.
**VOL-A-032** (F-004): Cancellation: the VP may cancel an objective at any state; the director marks it `cancelled`, posts a directive to every involved room, and downstream in-flight sends are closed as `deferred{reason: objective-cancelled}` (reason naming per §3.4 counters). Cancellation does not delete evidence: the room log and state record persist as control state.
**VOL-A-033** (F-004, D-016): A change of VP direction is a VP message into the objective room (CT-10/§11.1: inject messages into rooms it names). The director SHALL treat it as a criteria/decomposition revision: record the revision in control state, re-decompose affected assignments, and propagate changed conditions downward as a **recorded authorized change** (D-012/ F-013: conditions flow down unchanged *unless an authorized change is recorded*). In-flight work that the revision invalidates is re-scoped or cancelled per VOL-A-032 mechanics at the assignment level.

### 4.6 Cross-manager composition and separately delegated delivery (D-011)
**VOL-A-034** (F-004, D-011): The director can request work from different managers in sequence, then assign another manager to combine the reports into a summary artifact (e.g. HTML). Composition is a **separate assignment** with its own owner, its own report, and dependency links to every composed assignment; artifact lineage (which report/artifact fed which section) SHALL be recorded in the composing assignment's report artifacts. Artifact generation, acceptance, and delivery are separate stages (D-011 scope note).
**VOL-A-035** (F-004, D-011): Delivery is a distinct, delegable stage: the director may deliver if it is equipped (holds the configured communication capability itself), or delegate delivery through a communications manager to a supervisor with the configured capability to send the artifact to the human via the configured channel (Telegram is illustrative, not mandatory — D-011). An agent delivering to a human needs the *use* permission for that channel; an agent delegating delivery needs only the authority to assign the stage — use/grant distinction per VOL-A-008. No VP message-authorizing signal is implied by this spec: nothing is sent externally by this document's existence (D-011 scope; review Coverage note).

### 4.7 Aggregation and acceptance (D-010)
**VOL-A-036** (F-004, D-010): Manager-reported completion is NOT acceptance. When all owner managers of an objective report completion, the director SHALL start acceptance review: verify each completion against the objective's criteria (VP-supplied, director-derived, standing-rule — with provenance and per-criterion evidence; detail VOL-D F-013), apply persistent standing rules to applicable work (D-010; integration owned by Hermes learning per D-013, with effective-rule evidence required by acceptance — F-006/F-013 boundary), and only then mark the objective `accepted`. There is no universal acknowledgement rule (D-012); acceptance conditions come from the objective's criteria alone.
**VOL-A-037** (F-004, D-010, D-008): Where the VP configuration requires human approval for the director (D-008 approval policy), `accepted` is reachable only after that approval; explicit human-wait propagates upward, prior authorization can permit continuation, and explicit approval gates hold — silence and timeouts grant nothing (D-012). Timer/status contracts for waits are VOL-D (F-013); **waiting-interval defaults are OPEN DESIGN WORK** (§8, OW-4).

### 4.8 Wake-completion vs objective-completion
**VOL-A-038** (F-004): The two completions SHALL never be conflated: - **Wake completion**: one dispatched send closed by a fresh, verified report (CT-05/CT-06, RL-20) — the unit the verify loop and ladder operate on. - **Objective completion**: the lifecycle state `accepted`, reached only via §4.7 after all accountable owners report, composition and delivery stages close, and configured approvals hold. A verified report moves its send to terminal; it never moves the objective by itself. Conversely, an objective's acceptance requires evidence at every level — upstream reports feed the director's review (F-004 completion evidence: "one objective from VP request through multi-manager work and upstream evidence").

### 4.9 The blocked → escalated → granted/reassigned → resumed path, end to end
**VOL-A-039** (F-004, D-009, D-012, Q-004): The canonical blocked path SHALL preserve ownership and evidence at every hop: 1. Foreman/supervisor detects blocker → posts `status=blocked` report with evidence (VOL-A-030); keeps ownership. 2. Manager verifies the blocker is beyond its delegated scope (else it resolves it — VOL-A-004) → reports blocked upward to the director. 3. Director records `escalated`, then either: a. **reassigns** (VOL-A-031) — ownership moves with the evidence trail; or b. **grants** (VOL-A-009/010) — a director grant from the VP-authorized pool, provenance-recorded, enforceable at the VOL-C boundary; or c. **escalates to VP** — the needed authority exceeds the director's delegatable pool (D-009/D-016); or d. **waits for human** — the blocker is an explicit human-input gate (D-012): `awaiting-human`, propagated upward; prior authorization may permit continuation, an explicit approval gate holds. 4. On unblock, the resumed assignment continues with the same objective record, same room threads (history preserved in the log, R-025), and the blocked interval visible in evidence — resumed work never restarts as if untouched, and no duplicate work is created (F-013's duplicate/late rules, VOL-D). 5. Every hop writes a durable record (VOL-A-012, R-017).

### 4.10 Changed-requirement handling summary
**VOL-A-040** (F-004, D-012, D-016): Requirements change through exactly three doors: a VP direction change (VOL-A-033), a director criteria extension (VOL-A-027, D-010), or an authorized change recorded on a delegated assignment (D-012). All three produce versioned, provenance-carrying records; downstream assignments inherit changed conditions only through one of these doors. A manager or supervisor SHALL NOT originate a requirement change.

## 6. TRACED EXAMPLE SKELETON (acceptance-demonstration scaffold)
This skeleton is the structure the acceptance demonstration (handoff: "Trace a VP objective through multiple managers, conditional supervisor actions, foreman/worker execution, report composition and authorized user delivery") must instantiate. Every authority branch is named; each [A-n] marker cites the requirement that governs it.
**Objective.** VP (owner's Hermes surface, using its director-calling tool) sends: "Prepare the fleet release-readiness pack: infra status, release audit, and one HTML summary." [A: VP create-objectives grant, CT-10; room `obj-relpack` opened, `created` → `decomposing`]
1. **Director decomposition** [VOL-A-026]: director owns decomposition; it derives/extends acceptance criteria where the VP gave none [VOL-A-027, D-010]. Assignments: `mgr-infra` (infra status), `mgr-fleet-ops` (release audit), sequential dependency: composition depends on both [VOL-A-028]. Conditions passed down unchanged [D-012]. Decision owner: **director**. 2. **Manager task split** [VOL-A-004]: each manager commits task decisions within its delegated scope; `mgr-infra` opens task room `task-relpack-infra`, assigns `sup-crier`. Decision owner: **manager** (within scope). 3. **Supervisor conditional actions** [VOL-A-006/007]: `sup-crier` runs its written rules — gather lane health, run bounded probes, compare thresholds — and coordinates the foreman. It hits an ambiguous threshold → escalates to manager with evidence, decides nothing sideways. Decision owner: **supervisor executes rules only**. 4. **Foreman execution** [VOL-A-014..020, D-004]: foreman receives the assignment message, describes/adjusts the work, dispatches workers through the managed controller contract (board rows, worktrees), reallocates one stalled worker, and posts one final report with artifact refs (commit, board row, CI run). Decision owner: **foreman** for execution mechanics. 5. **Blocked branch** [VOL-A-039]: `mgr-fleet-ops`' audit assignment blocks — a needed check requires a capability the manager lacks. Manager reports blocked upward with evidence (keeps ownership). Director: - if VP authorized a grant pool covering the capability → **director grants it on demand** [VOL-A-009/010, D-009] — including the demonstration case where the director may grant a tool it cannot itself use [VOL-A-008]; - else → director escalates to VP [VOL-A-039.3c] or reassigns to a manager holding the capability [VOL-A-031]. Evidence trail preserved. 6. **Human-wait branch** [VOL-A-037, D-012]: one audit criterion requires owner sign-off → supervisor reports waiting-for-human; manager propagates; director sets `awaiting-human`; prior authorization lets unaffected work continue; the explicit approval gate itself holds — a timeout grants nothing. 7. **Report composition** [VOL-A-034, D-011]: both managers report completion (verified fresh reports, CT-06/RL-20 — a stale report for the wrong request closes nothing, F-013 evidence). Director assigns the composing manager; HTML artifact with lineage refs is produced; stage `composing`. 8. **Separately delegated delivery** [VOL-A-035, D-011]: director delegates delivery through the communications manager to a supervisor holding the configured send capability (use permission on the channel). Director needs no communication tool of its own (F-008 boundary). Stage `delivering`. 9. **Acceptance** [VOL-A-036/037, D-010]: director runs acceptance review against VP-supplied + derived + standing-rule criteria with per-criterion evidence; manager-reported completion ≠ acceptance; configured human approval (D-008) closes `accepted`. Objective completion ≠ any single wake completion [VOL-A-038]. 10. **Demonstration must also show** (handoff list): stored messages/thread ownership (R-025), session continuation NEW/REUSE (CT-04), caps/queue behavior (`queued`, VOL-A-029), duplicate/crash recovery (VOL-B/D, F-007/F-014), a fresh-timestamp report for the wrong request rejected (VOL-D, F-013/RL-20), VP-config precedence over a conflicting director delegation [VOL-A-010, D-016], and the grantor-authorized-for-what-it- cannot-use case [VOL-A-008].
